3476.prule: No positional rule. Hanke states explicitly that no definite rule for stress can be set up: in his count of 196 polysyllabic words, ultima and penult were stressed about equally often and 25 words on the antepenult, so the language 'prefers the last two syllables as bearers of the accent'. Stress is therefore lexically given per word (marked with an acute on cited forms), falling within the final three syllables, with no stated conditioning by weight or syllable count.

3478.prule: Dominant penultimate stress in routine speech, quantity-insensitive at word level: disyllables on the first syllable, trisyllables usually on the second (some trisyllables, especially those with vowel-dropping short forms, on the first); in words of four or more syllables with a monosyllabic stem the stress falls on the second syllable of the word, and in multisyllabic nominalized verb forms on the last syllable of the nominalized stem; emphasis/focus shifts stress to the final syllable (stress sandhi).

3484.heavy: Wangdi 2020: 407: 'a light syllable is any open syllable in which the rhyme is occupied by a short vowel... An open syllable in which the rhyme consists of either a long vowel or a diphthong is a heavy syllable. In other words, all closed syllables are heavy; and open syllables with long vowels or diphthongs are also heavy.' Wangdi 2021: 161 adds: 'a light syllable with no initial clusters is any open syllable... open syllables with long vowels or diphthongs or an open syllable with onset clusters are also heavy'; 2021: 185: light = monomoraic, heavy (long vowel, diphthong, CVC) = bimoraic.
3484.dflt: σ1 (light.light -> first syllable; heavy.heavy -> first syllable; heavy.light -> first syllable)
3484.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the phonological word unless the word is light.heavy (σ1 = open syllable with short vowel; σ2 = closed syllable, or long vowel / diphthong), in which case the heavy second syllable is stressed. Table 19 (thesis p. 178): L.L -> 1st, L.H -> 2nd, H.L -> 1st, H.H -> 1st. Primary stress is therefore always on σ1 or σ2. Stress is non-contrastive (delimitative); correlates: intensity chiefly, with higher pitch and length.
3484.srule: Disyllables carry only the primary stress; words of three or four syllables (roots, or stems made tri/quadrisyllabic by suffixes/enclitics) carry one secondary stress placed relative to the primary: primary on σ1 -> secondary on σ3 (final in trisyllables [ˈlə́ŋ.bɔ.ˌtɕʰe] 'elephant', penult in quadrisyllables [ˈkɔ.kɐ.ˌli.kɔ] 'crow'); primary on σ2 -> no secondary in trisyllables ([kʰɐ.ˈrək.pɐ] 'quiet'), secondary on final σ4 in quadrisyllables ([tɐ.ˈlɐi.zɪk.ˌpɐ] 'centipede'). No monomorphemic words longer than four syllables. Compounds/reduplications: each component stressed independently.

tn.quote: Brokpa has two register tones, distinguished by pitch height applied over a syllable within a phonological word. Syllables with obstruents have an inherent pitch value, whereas syllables beginning with sonorants are contrastive for pitch. ... In Brokpa, the voiceless stops have corresponding high pitch, and the voiced stops have corresponding low pitch and breathy voice on the vowel. Pitch in this context is not contrastive ... Pitch that follows sonorant consonants, however, is contrastive, and will be referred to as tone.
tn.cite: Wangdi, Pema. 2020. Segmental and suprasegmental features of Brokpa. Himalayan Linguistics 19(1): 393-422. DOI 10.5070/H919148641.
tn.locator: §3 'Tone', p. 403 (Table 11 'Contrastive tone on sonorant-initial words in Brokpa' p. 404)
tn.note: Two register tones, high vs low, contrastive only on sonorant-initial syllables; after obstruents pitch follows onset voicing. Separate non-contrastive weight-sensitive stress, cued partly by pitch.

3488.prule: No positional rule: the dedicated phonology (Margery 1996, 1.2.2, pp. 23-24) classifies Bocotá de Chiriquí as an accentual (stress) language 'of the so-called free-accent type' (una lengua acentual del tipo de las denominadas 'de acento libre'); accent = an increase in intensity on one syllable within the word (or, for monosyllables, within the clause); its distinctive function is shown by disyllabic and trisyllabic minimal pairs (/gú.dɛ/ 'comer': /gu.dɛ́/ 'felino', /dá.bɛ/ 'rojo': /da.bɛ́/ 'maduro', /hí.gɛ/ 'trampa': /hi.gɛ́/ 'largo', /ba.dá.da/ 'ave': /ba.da.dá/ 'nieto'); monosyllables divide into accented and unaccented when placed in a clause (/bá/ 'usted': /ba/ 'forma'). The 1992/1994 notes add that each polysyllabic word heard in isolation has one syllable perceived as prominent, and that the acute is written on the nucleus of the prominent/culminative syllable of tri- and tetrasyllables both in isolation and in the phrase, while for mono- and disyllables it follows the perceived phrasal accentuation. Position is not derivable from syllable count or weight.

tn.translation: Our description of the phonology of Chiriquí Bocotá specifies the existence of two suprasegmental phonemes: nasality and accent. ... Chiriquí Bocotá shows itself to be an accentual language. On this level, the accent is the increase in intensity that a syllable acquires within a word or, as will be seen below, in the context of a clause. ... [1989, n. 7] Bocotá, as far as our research in this field has reached, has revealed itself to us as a tonal language, of low functional yield, with two phonemic tones, one high and one low.

tn.note: The 1996 phonology sets up two suprasegmentals only, nasality and a free distinctive intensity accent, and no tone phoneme; the author's 1989 note had provisionally called Bocotá tonal (high/low).

3488.cfw: Margery Peña's 1996 phonology of the Chiriquí dialect calls it an accentual language of the free-accent type and his 1992 and 1994 text collections mark stress word by word, but he had called the same dialect tonal in 1989, Gunn and Gunn 1974 describe accent at the phrase level, Chevrier 2017 still lists Buglere among the Chibchan languages where tone versus accent has been an open question, and the 1996 article is known only from search excerpt, so lexical stress is the likely answer but it rests on one fieldworker's revised analysis.

Barbora 2025 abstract (paywalled) says its sketch covers 'the phonemic inventory, tone, and the syllabic structure'. No source reached describes stress or a pitch-accent rule; tonal status is asserted (Dondrup, Barbora) but contested (Lander-Portnoy).

tn.translation: Buli is a tone language in which relative pitch fulfils lexical as well as, to a high degree, grammatical function. … Examining the nominal domain of the lexicon, Buli yields the three tonemes high tone (H), mid tone (M) and low tone (L). There are, however, hardly any minimal triplets in which all three tonemes contrast in an identical environment. … Verbs have no distinctive lexical tone … Contour tones are not tonemes in Buli but arise from the combination of two tones on a single syllable.

3494.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word, non-contrastive, in words of one to five syllables (monomorphemic words of more than five syllables do not occur).
3494.srule: Secondary stress on the third syllable of four- and five-syllable monomorphemic words (jálungùrru 'good', bályamàrada 'motorcar'); words of one to three syllables have the primary only. 3495.srule: Words of four or more syllables break into groups of two or three syllables following the word's morphology (reduplicant, prefix, root, suffix), each group stressed: a 2-syllable group on its first syllable, a 3-syllable group on its first or second, i.e. a stress every second or third syllable ('hada'hada 2+2; '?ateni'yega 3+2, 'wanu'watuhu 2+3; 'to?u'to?u'pana 2+2+2, ?a'gudusu'?ani 3+3; 'lasa'lasaidi'yedi 2+2+3; words up to 12 syllables likewise). The primary stress is the last stressed syllable (the penult, often lengthened); the preceding group stresses are the non-primary ones. The source does not use the word 'secondary'.

3497.heavy: No heavy-syllable class is defined. Three attractors are named: (a) the vowel 'immediately before the conjunct consonant', i.e. a syllable closed by the first member of a cluster (bháddō 'ugly', rássī 'rope', bíddyā 'knowledge'); (b) 'a long ā vowel' in causative roots, 'always stressed' (karā́nō); (c) whichever of the last two syllables 'happens to be longer than the other'. Rule (i) adds that in a word with a consonantal ending 'from the point of view of pronunciation' (final written -a elided) the stress is on the penultimate vowel of the pronounced form, i.e. the syllable before the closed final one (kā́.gaj 'paper', sá.ṛak 'road'); a word-final closing consonant therefore does not make its syllable attract stress, whereas an internal cluster does.
3497.dflt: Not stated. Where the last two syllables are of equal length the illustrations go both ways -- penult in sakā́rē and sirahā́nō, final in kudārī́, barasātī́ and pichavāṛṓ -- and three examples stress a short vowel against a long neighbour (pácīsa, maṭákā, camārána), contrary to the 'longer' rule as transcribed; the author offers illustrations 'rather than descriptions' because of the 'lack of stability and regularity'.
3497.prule: Weight-conditioned, right-edge, and stated with hedges: in words of two to four syllables stress is 'usually on the last or the last but one, if it happens to be longer than the other'; in a word that ends in a consonant in pronunciation (final written -a elided) the stress is on the penultimate vowel of the pronounced form, i.e. the syllable before the closed final one (kā́.gaj 'paper', sá.ṛak 'road' -- a light penult is stressed rather than the closed final); the vowel immediately before a conjunct consonant is stressed (bháddō, rássī, bíddyā); the long ā of causative stems is always stressed (karā́nō, likhā́nō, baiṭhā́nō). Monosyllables have no stress in isolation. The author frames the whole system as weak, 'irregular', fluctuating 'in every word', and hard to separate from emphasis, and says the rules are Hindi's (Guru, Hindi Vyakaran § 56), 'some of which are also valid for Bundeli'. The illustrations as printed: final stress in kudārī́, dēkhabṓ, barasātī́, pichavāṛṓ and camārána (last syllable before the elided -a); penultimate stress in bhā́va, sakā́rē, sirahā́nō, and on a short penult in pácīsa and maṭákā.

3500.tone: The source says nothing about stress or accent: the words 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' do not occur in the 9-page paper, and in the four other saved Bura texts (Blench's 2010 dictionary draft, the mission 'Bura Grammar for a Beginner', Schuh's tone-marked Bura-English-Hausa dictionary, Maddieson 1983 SAL 14(3)) 'stress' appears only about English emphasis or as a gloss verb (Grammar sec. 5.5.2 'In English, this may be emphasised merely by a vocal stress upon the adjective'; Schuh 'bzà part. (clause final particle used by men to stress a proposition)') and in a bibliography title (Harris 1983 in Maddieson), never as a statement about Bura prosody. It states that Bura is a tone language whose system 'is yet to be fully worked out': Davies' three-way contrast (ká/ka/kà) is reinterpreted as two tones (H, L) plus downstep, with phonetic rising tone from vowel sequences and rare phonemic rising tone; the mark table lists High, Low, Falling, Rising. Sec. 1 adds that 'this paper provisionally eschews tone-marking'. Schuh's dictionary marks H, L and falling tone on every headword (e.g. tlâata) and notes deletion/reduction of one class of word-final vowels 'when not at the end of a phonological phrase', but gives no tone or stress analysis.
